CHAPTER 3: ECONOMIC, SOCIAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY
(Best studied together with Chapter 16.)

WHAT YOU SHOULD BE ABLE TO DO AFTER THIS CHAPTER
- Outline economic, social and environmental sustainability and explain how they are connected.
- Identify indicators of economic growth, social cohesion, inequality and environmental sustainability, and examine how they relate.
- Consider what sustainable development means for individual behaviour, choices, habits and values; business decisions; and government policy.

SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
- Sustainable development: development that meets the current needs of humankind without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
- It is concerned with people having satisfying lives and a healthy environment now and in the future.
- Unsustainable development: when present progress is achieved at the expense of future generations.
- To achieve economic growth, a government could allow or even encourage practices that are economically, environmentally and socially unsustainable. Growth should be achieved without harming society and the environment.

THE THREE ELEMENTS (PILLARS) OF SUSTAINABILITY (TABLE 3.1)
- Environmental sustainability: whether natural resources (gifts of nature) can be maintained into the future.
- Economic activity is environmentally sustainable if it does not: result in excess pollution; rely on non-renewable energy; damage ecosystems.
- Not environmentally sustainable: dumping plastic waste into the sea; clearing the Amazon Rainforest in Brazil (e.g. for agricultural land).
- Economic sustainability: making sure economic growth is not achieved at the expense of future generations.
- Example: it is not economically (or environmentally) sustainable to grow the economy while emitting high levels of greenhouse gases.
- Social sustainability: creating equal opportunities for all citizens on the planet, e.g. access to healthcare, education, income, water or food.

TABLE 3.2: ENVIRONMENTALLY UNSUSTAINABLE VS SUSTAINABLE
- Unsustainable: burning fossil fuels to generate electricity; continued use of petrol/diesel vehicles; production and use of single-use plastics.
- Sustainable: generating energy from solar and wind (e.g. wind turbines in Co. Wexford); using electric vehicles (EVs); recyclable packaging such as paper and cardboard.

TABLE 3.3: ECONOMICALLY UNSUSTAINABLE VS SUSTAINABLE
- Unsustainable: allowing large MNCs to keep paying very little corporation tax despite huge profits; using child labour in textile and mining industries to make goods sold cheaply in developed economies (economically and socially unsustainable).
- Sustainable: all members of society, including profitable MNCs, making a fair contribution to the state reflecting their ability to pay; economic activity without child labour that respects the human rights of all.
- National debt: the Department of Finance expected Ireland's national debt to rise to 47,700 euro per capita by the end of 2021. Continuously increasing national debt raises questions of economic sustainability.

TABLE 3.4: SOCIALLY UNSUSTAINABLE VS SUSTAINABLE
- Unsustainable: gender inequality, e.g. lower pay for women than men for the same work, or a lack of educational opportunities for girls; exploiting the resources indigenous people depend on, e.g. cutting down the Amazon Rainforest, damaging the long-term survival of indigenous communities.
- Sustainable: equal pay and equal treatment of men and women at work, and equal access to education for all; protecting the environments indigenous people depend on.

CLIMATE CHANGE
- Climate change is the most significant environmental challenge facing the planet today.
- It is caused by unsustainable human activities that emit greenhouse gases.
- Figure 3.1 shows the breakdown of US greenhouse gas emissions in 2018 (source: US EPA).
- The four main greenhouse gases:
- Carbon dioxide: the main greenhouse gas, emitted when fossil fuels are burnt.
- Methane: emitted in producing and transporting coal, natural gas and oil; also from livestock and certain agricultural practices.
- Nitrous oxide: from certain agricultural and industrial activities; vehicles are also a source.
- Fluorinated gases: potent greenhouse gases from a variety of industrial processes.
- Effects discussed: greenhouse gases trap heat; warmer oceans raise sea levels; ice caps are affected; extreme weather events.

THE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS (SDGs)
- In 2015, 193 countries agreed on 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The hope is that all nations will achieve all 17 by 2030.
- UN definition (un.org): the SDGs are a call for action by poor, rich and middle-income countries to promote prosperity while protecting the planet. Ending poverty must go hand-in-hand with strategies that build economic growth and address social needs (education, health, social protection, job opportunities) while tackling climate change and environmental protection.
- SDGs mentioned in the chapter: SDG 3 (health - the World Health Organization plays a central role); SDG 5 (gender equality); SDG 10 (reduced inequality); SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities); SDG 13 (climate action - the Paris Accord); SDG 16 (peace, justice and strong institutions).
- The SDGs are highly interconnected: policies for one goal advance others. E.g. policies for gender equality (SDG 5) also help reduce inequality (SDG 10), promote sustainable cities and communities (SDG 11) and build peace, justice and strong institutions (SDG 16).

WHAT INDIVIDUALS CAN DO
- 1. Reduce consumption of fossil fuels: replace a petrol/diesel car with an EV, use public transport, cycle, walk, fly less, insulate your home, install solar panels, use energy-saving light bulbs.
- 2. Reduce single-use plastics by choosing 'green' alternatives, e.g. biodegradable packaging, 'keep cups' for drinks.
- 3. Reduce food waste - why spend money on food only to throw it out?
- 4. Choose locally produced goods: an apple flown in from New Zealand involves significant greenhouse gas emissions in transport.
- 5. Buy items produced sustainably, e.g. Fairtrade logo goods, organic fruit and vegetables.
- 6. Avoid items produced unsustainably, e.g. clothing made with child labour; coffee from an MNC that does not pay bean suppliers a fair price.

WHAT FIRMS CAN DO
- 1. Offer environmentally sustainable options: paper/cardboard packaging instead of plastic; compostable coffee cups in coffee shops.
- 2. Stock only items made in a socially sustainable way: e.g. a textiles retailer should be confident fair wages are paid to factory workers and products are made safely.
- 3. Reduce greenhouse gas emissions: e.g. An Post switching to electric vehicles; Ryanair investing in new fuel-efficient planes that carry more passengers and use less fuel.

WHAT THE IRISH GOVERNMENT CAN DO (incentives, taxation, regulation and funding)
- Grants for electric vehicles (Chapter 7).
- Increase the carbon tax on fossil fuels (Chapter 7).
- Levies like the plastic bag levy, e.g. a 'latte levy' on disposable cups and a levy/tax on plastic bottles and packaging (Chapter 7).
- Policies to ensure gender equality (Chapter 9).
- Ensure safe working conditions - an issue in the Covid-19 pandemic regarding living and working conditions of non-EU workers in Irish meat factories.
- Prosecute individuals and firms that pollute.
- Fund recycling centres, recycling bins in public areas and information about recycling.
- Encourage/force state-owned companies to change: Bord na Mona has ended peat harvesting and is moving resources to renewable energy (solar and wind) and rehabilitating boglands; ESB closed two peat-burning power plants in 2020.

INDICATORS OF SUSTAINABILITY

1. GDP, GNP, GNI, GNDI
- National income: the income accruing to the permanent residents of a country from current (continuous) economic activity during a year.
- GDP, GNP, GNI and GNDI can be used to measure economic growth (definitions in Chapter 11).
- Example: GDP of 100 billion euro in Year 1 and 110 billion euro in Year 2 means the economy grew by 10%.
- But GDP does not measure sustainable development. GDP growth is often achieved at the expense of sustainability, e.g. by burning fossil fuels, polluting water, producing waste and exploiting workers.
- So a rise in GDP could show a country has grown in an unsustainable way. Better indicators are needed.

2. THE SOCIAL PROGRESS INDEX (SPI)
- A relatively new measure of the quality of life in countries.
- Uses over 50 indicators to give a score from 0 (no social progress) to 100 (full social progress).
- Three main areas: basic human needs; foundations of wellbeing; opportunity.
- Components (Figure 3.4): Basic human needs - nutrition and basic medical care, water and sanitation, shelter, personal safety. Foundations of wellbeing - access to basic knowledge (e.g. adult literacy rate), access to information and communications, health and wellness, environmental quality. Opportunity - personal rights, personal freedom and choice, inclusiveness, access to advanced education.
- SPI 2020 top: 1 Norway 92.73; 2 Denmark 92.11; 3 Finland 91.89; 4 New Zealand 91.64; 5 Sweden 91.62; 6 Switzerland 91.42; 7 Canada 91.40; 8 Australia 91.29; 9 Iceland 91.09; 10 Netherlands 91.06; 11 Germany 90.56; 12 Ireland 90.35; 13 Japan 90.14.
- SPI 2020 bottom: 151 Angola 48.16; 152 Guinea-Bissau 46.69; 153 Papua New Guinea 44.91; 154 Guinea 43.41; 155 Afghanistan 42.29; 156 DR Congo 42.25; 157 Niger 42.21; 158 Burundi 41.20; 159 Somalia 35.58; 160 Eritrea 35.20; 161 Central African Republic 31.62; 162 Chad 31.29; 163 South Sudan 31.06.
- So in 2020 Norway was the most successful at social progress and South Sudan the least. Ireland was 12th.
- Social progress and the SDGs are closely linked; social progress can be achieved by pursuing the SDGs.

3. THE HUMAN DEVELOPMENT INDEX (HDI) (more in Chapter 16)
- People generally aspire to: health (long and healthy lives); education (a good standard of education); income (a good standard of living).
- The HDI brings these three dimensions of human development together.
- Scale from 0 (no development) to 1 (full human development). The closer to 0, the less developed.
- 2019: Norway 1st (0.957), Ireland 2nd (0.955), Niger last (0.394).

4. THE INEQUALITY-ADJUSTED HDI (IHDI)
- Economic inequality: the unequal distribution of income and opportunity between different groups in a society.
- The IHDI takes the HDI one step further: it combines a country's average achievements in health, education and income with how those achievements are distributed among the population.
- Inequalities reflected: access to healthcare; access to education; distribution of income (e.g. 10% of the population controlling 60% of the wealth).
- Causes: income inequality (high earners can afford private healthcare or school/university; low earners cannot); gender inequality (e.g. males getting education while females do not).
- If HDI equals IHDI, there is no inequality. The further apart they are, the greater the inequality.

5. THE GINI COEFFICIENT (GINI INDEX)
- Measures inequality of income distribution in a region or country.
- Scale 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100).
- 0 = perfect equality of income (everyone has the same income).
- 1 (or 100) = perfect inequality of income (one individual earns all the income).
- Ireland 2019: 0.288 (28.8%). UK 2018: 0.37 (37%). So the UK had more income inequality.
- Government measures to reduce income inequality:
- A progressive tax system that takes proportionally more from higher earners; revenue is redistributed to those on lower incomes through social welfare.
- Education: central to a person's life chances and future earnings. The Irish Government provides free primary and secondary education and maintenance grants for third-level students from households below an income threshold.

OTHER DATA SOURCES
- World Inequality Database (wid.world): e.g. share of national income held by the richest 1% or 10%; useful for the research project.
- Eurostat (ec.europa.eu): EU progress on the SDGs; compare Ireland with other countries.
- Central Statistics Office (cso.ie): 'sustainable development indicators' and a breakdown of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions.
- Environmental Protection Agency (epa.ie): data on Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions.
- The MCC carbon clock (mcc-berlin.net): how much CO2 can still be released to limit warming to 1.5 degrees C and 2 degrees C, and tonnes of CO2 released every second.

CHALLENGES IN ACHIEVING THE SDGs
- Global social cohesion (solidarity among the nations of the world) is needed, but there are barriers:
- 1. Lack of political will: the US under President Trump withdrew from the Paris Accord (aimed at limiting global warming, SDG 13) and indicated it would leave the World Health Organization (central to SDG 3); President Biden reversed these in 2021. Authorities in Brazil encouraged/facilitated destruction of the Amazon Rainforest.
- 2. Funding: e.g. providing clean water and sanitation where they do not exist is expensive.
- 3. Corruption: funding for development projects can be misappropriated.
- 4. Lack of corporate social responsibility: firms stock products made with child labour or made in unsafe conditions by very low-paid workers.
- 5. Limited awareness: individuals may be unaware of, or uninterested in, how their goods/services are produced.

THE KUZNETS ENVIRONMENTAL CURVE (ENVIRONMENTAL KUZNETS CURVE) (FIGURE 3.7)
- Shows the relationship between environmental damage and the level of wealth in a country.
- Diagram in words: vertical axis = environmental damage; horizontal axis = per capita income. The curve is an upside-down U. Damage rises as income rises (environmental decay), reaches a peak at the 'turning point income', then falls as income keeps rising (environmental improvement).
- ENVIRONMENTAL DECAY (left side) - damage rises as an economy first expands, due to:
- Rapid industrialisation: fast growth of manufacturing brings high pollution.
- Urbanisation: rapid growth of urban centres harms the environment if not managed and infrastructure is not provided.
- Poor government regulation: polluters face few or no consequences.
- ENVIRONMENTAL IMPROVEMENT (right side) - damage falls after the turning point income, due to:
- Higher incomes: consumers can afford more expensive 'greener' products, e.g. organic fruit and vegetables.
- Structural change: manufacturing (high-polluting) becomes less important and services (low-polluting) more important.
- Technological improvements linked to growth: solar and wind energy, cleaner production techniques, electric vehicles.
- Government intervention to overcome market failures that cause pollution: regulations restricting pollution, and taxes/levies on polluting goods (e.g. carbon taxes).

Growing GDP as fast as possible each year
Using only renewable energy in industry

rows.prompt: State the three elements of sustainability and give one example of each.
rows.model_answer: Environmental sustainability - maintaining natural resources, e.g. generating energy from wind and solar. Economic sustainability - growth not at the expense of future generations, e.g. all firms including MNCs paying a fair share of tax. Social sustainability - equal opportunities for all, e.g. equal pay and equal access to education for men and women.

rows.prompt: Name the four main greenhouse gases and one source of each.
rows.model_answer: Carbon dioxide - burning fossil fuels. Methane - producing and transporting coal, gas and oil, and livestock. Nitrous oxide - certain agricultural and industrial activities and vehicles. Fluorinated gases - a variety of industrial processes.

rows.prompt: State four choices a consumer can make to contribute to sustainable development.
rows.model_answer: Reduce fossil fuel use, e.g. switch to an EV, cycle or use public transport; reduce single-use plastics, e.g. use a keep cup; reduce food waste; buy locally produced goods; buy Fairtrade or organic goods; avoid goods made with child labour.

rows.prompt: Outline three ways the Irish Government can encourage sustainable development.
rows.model_answer: It can give grants for electric vehicles, raise the carbon tax on fossil fuels, and introduce levies like the plastic bag levy (e.g. a latte levy). It can also prosecute polluters, fund recycling, ensure safe working conditions and direct state companies like Bord na Mona and ESB to move away from peat.

rows.prompt: Does a rise in GDP mean economic activity is increasing in a sustainable way? Explain.
rows.model_answer: No. GDP measures economic growth but not sustainable development. Growth is often achieved by burning fossil fuels, polluting water, producing waste and exploiting workers, so a rise in GDP could show the economy grew in an unsustainable way.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between the HDI and the IHDI.
rows.model_answer: The HDI combines a country's achievements in health, education and income on a scale of 0 to 1. The IHDI adjusts the HDI to take account of how those achievements are distributed, e.g. unequal access to healthcare, education and income. If the two figures are equal there is no inequality; the bigger the gap, the more inequality.

rows.prompt: Country A has a Gini coefficient of 0.72 and Country B 0.43. Which is closer to perfect inequality and which to perfect equality? Explain.
rows.model_answer: Country A (0.72) is closer to perfect inequality, because 1 means one person earns all the income. Country B (0.43) is closer to perfect equality, because 0 means everyone has the same income.

rows.prompt: Describe the Kuznets Environmental Curve in words.
rows.model_answer: Environmental damage is on the vertical axis and per capita income on the horizontal axis. Damage rises as income first grows (environmental decay) due to industrialisation, urbanisation and poor regulation. It peaks at the turning point income, then falls (environmental improvement) due to greener spending, a shift to services, new technology and government intervention.

rows.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the Kuznets Environmental Curve. Outline the reasons for environmental decay and environmental improvement as a country's income rises. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram: vertical axis labelled environmental damage, horizontal axis labelled per capita income. An inverted U-shaped curve rises (environmental decay), peaks at the 'turning point income', then falls (environmental improvement). Environmental decay: (1) Rapid industrialisation - fast growth of manufacturing brings high pollution. (2) Urbanisation - fast-growing urban centres damage the environment if growth is unmanaged and infrastructure is lacking. (3) Poor government regulation lets polluters pollute without significant consequences. Environmental improvement: (1) Higher incomes let consumers afford dearer 'greener' products, e.g. organic food. (2) Structural change - high-polluting manufacturing falls in importance while low-polluting services grow. (3) Technological improvements such as solar and wind energy, cleaner production techniques and EVs. (4) Government intervention to correct market failures, e.g. pollution regulations and carbon taxes.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram: 5 marks (axes 2 marks, inverted U with turning point income labelled 3 marks). Reasons: 4 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation), at least one decay and one improvement reason.

rows.prompt: (a) Explain the Gini coefficient. (b) Outline two measures a government could take to reduce income inequality. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) The Gini coefficient measures inequality of income distribution in a region or country on a scale of 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100). A figure of 0 means perfect equality - everyone has the same income. A figure of 1 means perfect inequality - one individual earns all the income. In 2019 Ireland's figure was 0.288, while the UK's 2018 figure was 0.37, showing greater inequality in the UK. (b) (1) A progressive tax system takes proportionally more from higher earners, and the revenue is redistributed to lower-income people through social welfare. (2) Education is central to life chances and future earnings, so the government provides free primary and secondary education and maintenance grants to third-level students from lower-income households.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 5 marks (2 + 3), with reference to scale and meaning of 0 and 1. (b) 2 measures x 5 marks (2 + 3).

rows.prompt: Discuss the implications of sustainable development for (i) individuals, (ii) firms and (iii) the government. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) Individuals can change their behaviour, choices and habits: reduce fossil fuel use by switching to an EV, using public transport, cycling, insulating homes and installing solar panels; reduce single-use plastics with keep cups; reduce food waste; buy local goods to avoid transport emissions; buy Fairtrade and organic goods and avoid goods made with child labour. (ii) Firms can offer sustainable options such as cardboard packaging and compostable cups; stock only goods made with fair wages and safe conditions; and reduce emissions, e.g. An Post switching to EVs and Ryanair buying fuel-efficient planes. (iii) The government can use incentives, taxes, regulation and funding: EV grants, higher carbon taxes, levies like the latte levy, gender equality policies, safe working conditions, prosecuting polluters, funding recycling, and directing Bord na Mona and ESB away from peat.
rows.marking_scheme: 4 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation). At least one point for each of individuals, firms and government required.

rows.prompt: State and explain three challenges in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: 1. Lack of political will: some leaders are less committed, e.g. the US under President Trump withdrew from the Paris Accord and indicated it would leave the WHO, and authorities in Brazil facilitated destruction of the Amazon. 2. Funding: providing basics such as clean water and sanitation where they do not exist requires large sums of money. 3. Corruption: in some nations funding for development projects is misappropriated. Other challenges include a lack of corporate social responsibility (firms stocking goods made with child labour) and limited consumer awareness of how goods are produced.
rows.marking_scheme: 3 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation).
